title: An Honest Audit of Every Way to Pay in Colombia (I Tried Them All So You Don't Have To)
summary: Pay local merchants by QR code across Asia and Latin America. Connect your bank or card, skip ATM fees, and pay like a local in your own currency with Moreta.
body_markdown:
Ask ten nomads in Medellín how to pay in Colombia and you will get ten confident, contradictory answers. "Cash is king, always carry pesos." "Never carry pesos, that's how you get targeted." "Just use your card everywhere." "Never use your card, it'll get cloned." "Get Nequi." "You can't get Nequi."


The frustrating part is that every one of those answers is partly true. Colombia in 2026 is a country mid-transition: the QR sticker economy built around Nequi, Daviplata, and Bancolombia has spread from big-city counters to neighborhood tiendas, while cash still runs plenty of daily life and foreign cards sit in an awkward middle zone. So instead of one more hot take, here is an actual audit. Four ways to handle everyday spending in Colombia, weighed honestly, with the verdict left to the evidence.


### Cash: still functional, increasingly inconvenient


Pesos work everywhere, full stop. The arepa stand outside your coworking space, the guy selling mango biche from a cart, the bus in a small Boyacá town. If your plan includes places where the QR stickers thin out, you will want some cash on hand.


The problems start at the ATM. Withdrawal limits per transaction mean a nomad burning through a monthly budget makes repeated trips, each with its own fee from the local machine plus whatever your home bank adds. Then there is the part nobody loves saying out loud: standing at a street ATM in an unfamiliar barrio, counting a fat stack of fifty mil notes, is exactly the moment every safety guide tells you to avoid. Colombians themselves have been moving away from carrying cash for this reason, which is a big part of why the QR wallets took off in the first place.


**Cash wins:** rural areas, street food in smaller towns, tipping, backup for outages.
**Cash loses:** ATM fee stacking, safety optics, the sheer logistics of resupply.


### Your foreign card: welcome in fewer places than you'd think


Here is the thing that surprises people who arrive from Europe or the US expecting tap-to-pay everywhere: Colombia never fell in love with the card terminal. Card cloning was a real and well-publicized problem here, and it left a mark on local habits. Many small merchants either never got a datáfono or quietly stopped using it, because their customers stopped trusting it. When you do pay by card at a restaurant, you will get the famous "¿cuántas cuotas?" question (how many installments), a local financing quirk that means nothing for you but confuses every first-timer. Answer "una" and move on.


Where cards do work reliably: chain supermarkets like Éxito and Carulla, malls, hotels, upscale restaurants in Bogotá's Zona G or Medellín's Provenza. Where they quietly fail: the lunch spot with the corrientazo menu, your local fruit vendor, the laundry service, the empanada window, and a striking number of cafés in supposedly modern neighborhoods where the counter says "efectivo o transferencia" and the terminal is nowhere to be seen.


**Cards win:** big-ticket, big-brand purchases.
**Cards lose:** most of the small daily transactions that make up actual nomad life, plus foreign transaction fees on many home-country cards.


### Local wallets: perfect, if you can get one


Nequi, Daviplata, and Bancolombia's QR system are how Colombians actually pay each other and pay merchants. The stickers are on almost every counter in Medellín's Laureles and El Poblado, all over Bogotá, and increasingly in Cali, Bucaramanga, and the coffee axis. Locals scan, transfer, done. No card, no cloning risk, no change fumbling. If you have ever watched the line at a busy panadería move at double speed because everyone is scanning instead of counting coins, you understand why Colombia loves this system. We broke down[how to tell the three main QR networks apart](https://moretapay.com/blog/colombia-qr-payments-nequi-daviplata-bancolombia-visitor-walkthrough-2026-2026-09-05) in an earlier piece if the sticker wall confuses you.


The catch for visitors is access. These wallets are built around Colombian identity documents and Colombian phone numbers. A tourist on a ninety-day stamp generally cannot open one, and even nomads on longer visas often find the onboarding assumes a cédula they do not have. Some travelers try workarounds involving a friend's account, which works right up until it becomes a favor you are asking weekly.


**Local wallets win:** on everything, if you qualify.
**Local wallets lose:** at the sign-up screen, for most readers of this blog.


### Scanning the same QR codes without the Colombian paperwork


This is the gap Moreta Pay exists to fill. It reads the same merchant QR codes that Nequi, Daviplata, and Bancolombia users scan, but the money comes from a wallet you topped up from your own bank back home (US bank via Plaid or ACH, SEPA in Europe, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer) or from an international card. You scan the sticker on the counter, see the amount, the merchant name, and the exact FX rate before you confirm, and the merchant gets paid instantly in pesos. From their side of the counter, it looks like any other QR transfer, which matters in a country where merchants trust the QR far more than they trust a foreign card.


No Colombian bank account, no cédula, no borrowed Nequi login. The tradeoff is honest too: Moreta Pay only helps where there is a QR code to scan. It will not buy you a mango from a cart with no sticker, and it will not replace cash in the countryside. It is a tool for the QR economy, which happens to be exactly where most of a city-based nomad's spending lives.


### The verdict, situation by situation


Rather than crown one winner, here is how the audit actually shakes out for a month of real life in Colombia:


-


**Daily food, coffee, markets, laundry, small services in Medellín, Bogotá, or Cali:** QR, every time. Use Moreta Pay to scan the same stickers locals do.


-


**Supermarket runs and mall purchases:** card or QR, whichever is cheaper for you after your card's foreign fees.


-


**Weekend trips to pueblos and rural fincas:** carry cash, more than you think you need.


-


**Online bookings on platforms like Trip.com or Agoda, and bills in supported countries:** QR-based checkout works here too, so your wallet covers more than street-level spending.


-


**Late-night anything:** QR beats pulling out a wallet full of bills, which is precisely why locals prefer it.


The pattern is the same one we found living[a full month in Brazil on Pix](https://moretapay.com/blog/brazil-digital-nomad-monthly-spending-pix-everyday-guide-2026-2026-09-10) : the local QR system is the center of gravity, cash is the fallback, and the foreign card is a supporting actor at best. Colombia without cash entirely is not realistic yet. Colombia with dramatically less cash, and no dependence on a card the merchant does not want anyway, absolutely is.
